strengths: Timely and reasonable research question: adapting masked diffusion LLMs to offline BBO to exploit bidirectional dependencies, moving beyond the prevailing autoregressive prompting paradigm (Section 2.3).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 16 baselines spanning forward, inverse, autoregressive, and diffusion families, four Design-Bench tasks, 8 random seeds, and consistent margins on three of four tasks (Table 1, e.g., +0.108 on TF Bind 8 over the best baseline).

Thorough ablations: delimiter tokens (Table 2), training-stage removal (Table 3), similarity-conditioned context (Table 4), and hyperparameter sensitivity including prompt-template robustness (Figure 2), which together support the pipeline design.

Reasonable methodological details: the one-step unmasking log-probability approximation for RL (Eq. 6) and the omission of clipping/KL under the uniform old-policy assumption are clearly motivated and grounded in prior work (Zhao et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2025).

Good transparency on setup: data partitioning strategy that prevents leakage (Appendix A.2), full prompt templates (Appendix A.3), single-GPU training time, and an honest acknowledgment that D'Kitty underperforms the best baseline.
Impact statement addresses misuse risks (e.g., biochemical design) and appropriately frames the tool as augmenting expert judgment.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim—that bidirectional modeling is what drives the gains—is never directly tested. The paper lacks the decisive control: an autoregressive LLM of comparable scale (e.g., fine-tuned LLaMA-3-8B) trained with the same DA + SFT + RL pipeline. The only AR comparison (OPRO) is a frozen prompting baseline, so the observed improvements could stem from the post-training pipeline or the base model rather than bidirectionality.

The 'state-of-the-art' claim is weaker than presented: on the median (50th-percentile) results in Table 5, DiBO is not best on D'Kitty (0.837 vs. 0.887 for COMs) or TF Bind 8 (0.599 vs. 0.623 for Grad-mean), suggesting the headline 100th-percentile best-of-128 metric inflates the advantage. The text (Appendix A.4) overstates the median results as SOTA.

The similarity-conditioned context construction yields an enormous ablation gap (0.730 → 0.965 on TF Bind 8, Table 4), indicating that much of the performance may come from careful retrieval of locally similar contexts rather than the diffusion modeling or RL itself; the paper does not disentangle or analyze this mechanism.

Limited task coverage: only four tasks, all from Design-Bench small-data settings; tasks commonly used in the literature (GFP, UTR, superconductor, NAS) are omitted, and the few-shot context cap of 7 due to memory constraints limits scalability claims.

Methodological novelty is modest: the components (delimiter-token domain adaptation, SFT via masked-response prediction, one-step RL for diffusion LLMs) are individually well-established; the contribution is primarily a successful adaptation, and the concurrent inference-only diffusion LLM work (Yuan et al., 2026) is excluded from the main comparison citing a regime mismatch, which weakens the positioning.

The RL reward r(q,o)=y(o)−y(q) is computed from labels of offline training designs, so the RL stage essentially re-weights known high-label data; the paper's framing of 'fine-grained reward feedback' overstates what is a form of label-aware resampling, and no analysis is given of whether generated designs are genuinely novel vs. near copies of training responses.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well organized, with a coherent three-stage pipeline (domain adaptation, SFT, RL) and a unified prompt-response corpus with delimiter tokens that is a reasonable engineering contribution for adapting diffusion LLMs to heterogeneous BBO inputs.

Comprehensive baselines: ten prior methods spanning forward, inverse (VAE/GAN/AR/diffusion), and evolutionary approaches are compared on Design-Bench, with 8 random seeds and both mean (Table 1) and median (Table 5) metrics reported.

The ablation studies are reasonably thorough: delimiter tokens (Table 2), individual training stages (Table 3), similarity-conditioned context (Table 4), and hyperparameter sensitivity including prompt-template variation (Figure 2) are all examined, which supports the internal validity of the pipeline design.

The appendix provides sufficient implementation detail (data construction, prompt templates, partitioning strategy, hyperparameters) for others to attempt reproduction, and code is promised to be released.
weaknesses: The central motivating hypothesis is never validated. The paper claims AR LLMs are 'insufficient' for design problems with bidirectional dependencies and that diffusion LLMs fix this, but there is no experiment demonstrating that bidirectionality is what drives the gains. The decisive missing control is fine-tuning a comparable-scale autoregressive LLM (e.g., LLaMA-3-8B, whose prompting variant OPRO is the only AR baseline) under the exact same unified corpus, SFT, and RL pipeline. Without this, the claimed mechanism is speculative, and the alternative explanation—that gains come from the similarity-conditioned context plus heavy fine-tuning of an 8B prior—is not ruled out. Table 4 itself shows the similarity-conditioned context alone yields up to +0.235, suggesting the framework may be dominated by local interpolation between prompt and response rather than bidirectional reasoning.

The evaluation scope is narrow relative to the claims. 'State-of-the-art on Design-Bench' is claimed, but only 4 of the many Design-Bench tasks (TF8, TF10, Ant, D'Kitty) are evaluated; standard tasks such as UTR, GFP, ChEMBL, and NASBench are omitted. On one of the four tasks (D'Kitty) the method actually loses to ExPT, and margins on several tasks are small relative to reported stds, with no statistical significance testing.

The RL formulation is technically questionable. Eq. (7) is a reward-weighted likelihood (multiplying the probability, not the log-probability, by r/σ), and the one-step unmasking approximation in Eq. (6) assumes response tokens are conditionally independent given a fully masked response—directly contradicting the paper's own motivation that design tokens exhibit strong dependencies. The tension between these modeling choices and the bidirectionality argument is not discussed.

The method's effective mechanism risks reducing to imitation of high-label dataset designs: SFT responses are drawn from the top-scored 20% of the offline pool (Appendix A.2), so the model is largely trained to reproduce known high-scoring designs conditioned on similar contexts. The paper does not analyze whether generated designs are genuinely novel or how much of the improvement is memorization/interpolation of the pool's upper tail.

Novelty is modest. The components (masked diffusion SFT, one-step log-probability RL from d1/dSFT-style recipes, tokenizer extension) are largely assembled from existing techniques; the contribution is primarily an application of diffusion LLM post-training to a new domain rather than a new method or new understanding.

No limitations section is provided; concerns such as the reliance on a large pretrained prior versus lightweight task-specific methods, compute cost relative to simpler baselines, and the small-data regime claims (N=500, which is not that small) are not candidly discussed. The impact statement touches on misuse but not on methodological limitations.

Fairness concerns across model capacity: DiBO fine-tunes an 8B pretrained LLM while most baselines train small task-specific models from scratch, making the comparison partly a statement about pretrained priors rather than about diffusion-versus-AR modeling or the proposed pipeline.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem (offline BBO with limited labeled data) and is, to my knowledge, among the first to *fine-tune* diffusion LLMs for this setting rather than only prompting them, building naturally on LLADA and recent dLLM RL techniques (e.g., d1, srft).

The proposed pipeline is sensible and clearly described: delimiter tokens to mark designs/labels, joint prompt–response masked reconstruction for domain adaptation, SFT on responses, and reward-weighted RL using label improvement as reward. The one-step unmasking approximation for log-probabilities is a practical and defensible efficiency choice.

Evaluation is reasonably broad: four Design-Bench tasks spanning discrete (TF Bind 8/10) and continuous (Ant, D'Kitty) domains, ten diverse baselines including surrogate, VAE/GAN/AR/diffusion methods, 8 random seeds with mean±std, plus median (50th percentile) results in the appendix that corroborate the headline 100th-percentile results.

Ablations are thorough and genuinely informative: delimiter tokens (Table 2), each training stage (Table 3, including the interesting finding that RL-only fails entirely on Ant), similarity-conditioned context construction (Table 4), and sensitivity analyses over context length, pool size, RL learning rate, and prompt templates (including GPT-generated template variants), which mitigates 'prompt hacking' concerns.

Reproducibility is above average: implementation details (optimizer, precision, learning rates, batch sizes, hardware, runtime), full prompt templates, data construction rules (partitioning, RBF-kernel similarity, median bandwidth), and a code release are provided. The impact statement honestly discusses bias inheritance and biochemical misuse risks.
weaknesses: The central motivating claim — that AR models are 'insufficient to fully capture bidirectional dependencies' and that bidirectionality is the source of the gains — is never directly tested. The only AR LLM baseline (OPRO with LLaMA3-8B-Instruct) is purely prompt-based, with no fine-tuning. A fine-tuned AR LLM with the same DA+SFT+RL pipeline (or a masked/insertion variant) is the obvious control and is missing, so the observed gains may come from fine-tuning and the reward signal rather than from bidirectionality.

Memorization vs. genuine optimization is not analyzed, and this is a serious confound. SFT responses are drawn from the top-20% slice of the same 500-sample offline pool used at test time, and the best-of-128-candidates metric rewards reproducing high-label designs. The paper never checks whether generated designs are novel (e.g., overlap/distance to the offline pool, or diversity of the 128 candidates), nor does it evaluate designs outside the pool distribution. The dramatic gain on Ant (0.944 vs. best-in-dataset 0.565) and the huge drop when random context replaces similar context on TF Bind 8 (0.730 vs. 0.965) are both consistent with local interpolation/regurgitation of pool designs rather than learned optimization structure.

Scale and scope of evidence is narrow: only four Design-Bench tasks (two of which, TF Bind 8/10, are tiny 8/10-length discrete spaces where bidirectional structure claims are weakly testable), no materials or UTR tasks from the same benchmark, and a single base model (LLADA-8B-Instruct). Generalization claims in the conclusion ('general-purpose paradigm for offline optimization') overreach relative to this evidence.

The RL formulation (uniform old-policy assumption, no clipping, no KL regularization, uncentered rewards normalized only by std) is borrowed from settings where such choices were motivated differently; there is no analysis of training stability beyond a learning-rate sweep, and no discussion of potential reward hacking or distribution collapse, which matters given the model is rewarded on labels of designs from its own training pool.

Several evaluation details are underspecified: how the 128 candidates are sampled at inference (schedule, temperature, number of denoising steps), how continuous designs rendered as 3-decimal text are parsed and scored by the oracle, and why only 7 few-shot examples are used despite npool=500 — all of which affect interpretation and reproducibility.

Positioning relative to the very closely related concurrent work (Yuan et al., 2026, diffusion LLMs for BBO) is thin: the direct comparison is relegated to a qualitative appendix note on the grounds of different few-shot regimes (npool=10 vs. 500), without an experiment adapting either method to the other's setting, even though both operate on Design-Bench.
Limitations are not consolidated: the D'Kitty underperformance, reliance on oracle-scored pools, and the memorization risk deserve an explicit limitations discussion rather than scattered remarks.

strengths: Well-motivated core idea: adapting diffusion LLMs (bidirectional modeling) to offline BBO, addressing a plausible weakness of AR LLM-based generators; the paper clearly positions itself against both forward (surrogate) and inverse (generative) methods.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 4 Design-Bench tasks plus 3 RNA tasks, 10 diverse baselines including recent LLM-based methods (OPRO, dLLM, MCTS-transfer), 8 random seeds, mean and median (100th/50th percentile) metrics, and Top-K metrics.

Strong and relevant ablations, most notably the matched diffusion-vs-AR backbone comparison (Table 2) that isolates the architectural claim while holding prompt construction, data, and pipeline fixed; plus ablations of delimiter tokens, training stages, similarity-conditioned context, and sub-sampling strategy.

Thoughtful reproducibility practices: full hyperparameters, prompt templates, corpus construction details, and a notable pretraining-overlap audit (Appendix A.7) that behaviorally probes whether LLADA-8B already encodes benchmark design-label knowledge — a concern often ignored in LLM-for-BBO work.

Thorough hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (few-shot count, pool size, RL learning rate, prompt paraphrases), and a fair treatment of GP baselines via dimension-scaled priors (Appendix A.4) that strengthens the baselines rather than weakening them.
weaknesses: Narrow primary benchmark: the main claims rest on only 4 Design-Bench tasks, and the auxiliary RNA results (Table 11) are mixed — DiBO is clearly behind on RNA-B and on Top-10/Top-20/median metrics for RNA-A/C — which tempers the generality claim of a 'robust, general-purpose paradigm'.

Reliance on the 100th-percentile (best-of-128) oracle metric, which is known on Design-Bench to reward methods that exploit surrogate-free generation near dataset maxima; while median results are reported and support the ranking, the headline SOTA claim is partly driven by this exploitable metric.

The RL formulation is weakly justified: the uniform old-policy assumption, removal of ratio clipping and KL regularization, and the one-step unmasking log-probability approximation (Eq. 6) are adopted rather than analyzed. There is no evidence that the one-step approximation yields valid policy gradients for masked diffusion models, and no comparison to alternative dLLM RL objectives (e.g., with iterative denoising estimates).

Potential conflation of contributions: Table 5 shows similarity-conditioned context construction alone yields +0.235 on TF Bind 8, suggesting data curation, not diffusion modeling, drives a large share of the gains. While the matched AR comparison controls for this, the paper does not disentangle how much of the SOTA margin over non-LLM baselines (e.g., ExPT) comes from the curated prompt-response corpus versus the backbone.

Novelty is moderate: the pipeline combines known components (tokenizer extension + domain adaptation, masked-response SFT, and dLLM RL following Zhao et al. 2025) applied to a new domain; the conceptual advance beyond existing diffusion-LLM RL and LLM-for-BBO literature is incremental.

Minor presentation issues: Eq. 3's indicator using a comma (conjunction of prompt and response masking) is ambiguous relative to Eq. 2, the reward dataset construction description is spread across Sections 3.2/Appendix A.2-A.3 making it hard to follow, and there is no dedicated limitations section (limitations are only implicitly addressed via the impact statement).

strengths: The paper addresses a timely question—whether diffusion LLMs can outperform autoregressive LLMs for offline black-box optimization—and situates it within a broad literature on both surrogate/generative BBO methods and diffusion LLM post-training.

The experimental protocol is unusually thorough for this area: 10 diverse baselines across forward, inverse, AR-LLM, and diffusion categories, 8 random seeds, median and Top-K reporting beyond the common 100th-percentile metric, hyperparameter sensitivity studies (few-shot count, pool size, learning rate, prompt paraphrases), and additional RNA tasks.

The pretraining-overlap audit (Appendix A.7, ranking probing against the random baseline) is a commendable and uncommon effort to rule out benchmark contamination from the pretrained LLADA checkpoint.

The matched backbone comparison (Table 2), delimiter-token ablation (Table 3), and stage ablation (Table 4) are the right kinds of ablations for the paper's central claims, and the DA stage ablation shows real value of domain adaptation (e.g., RL-only fails to produce valid outputs).
The appendix provides detailed prompt templates, data construction (disjoint D1/D2 partitioning, similarity-based context selection), and implementation specifics that support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central hypothesis—that bidirectional modeling is the key advantage for BBO—is asserted rather than demonstrated. No analysis is provided showing that the benchmark tasks actually exhibit significant suffix-dependencies (e.g., ablation of context masking, attention analysis, or a task where bidirectionality should matter most). The matched AR comparison shows gains of only 0.001–0.018 on continuous tasks and, notably, even the AR baseline reaches 0.915–0.934 after the same pipeline on TF Bind 8/Ant, suggesting the pipeline, not bidirectionality, drives most of the performance. On an 8-token DNA sequence, the bidirectionality argument is particularly unconvincing.

Methodological novelty is limited: the framework is a straightforward composition of known ingredients—continued pretraining/domain adaptation on a templated corpus, masked-response SFT, and a d1-style one-step RL objective with the uniform-old-policy assumption borrowed from prior work. The contributions (delimiter tokens, similarity-based context construction) are engineering choices rather than new techniques.

The RL objective in Eq. (7) is essentially advantage-weighted SFT under the uniform behavior-policy assumption; no clipping, KL regularization, or off-policy correction is analyzed, and the theoretical justification for the uniform-old-policy assumption in an offline BBO setting where designs come from arbitrary real-world processes is thin. There is no discussion of what this objective optimizes beyond one gradient step or of mode collapse risk.

The similarity-conditioned context construction (Table 5) is a major confound: it alone accounts for a 0.235 gain on TF Bind 8—far larger than the diffusion-vs-AR gap (0.050–0.080). The headline claim that bidirectional modeling enables the gains is therefore not well isolated; a simpler explanation is that careful context curation plus the post-training pipeline does the heavy lifting.

The evaluation metric (100th percentile of 128 oracle-scored candidates) is known to reward methods that exploit oracle extrapolation errors, and the paper does not discuss this risk. On median and several Top-K metrics (Table 10, 11), DiBO's advantage narrows or disappears (e.g., D'Kitty median 0.837 vs. COMs 0.887), and on the RNA tasks DiBO underperforms simple baselines on most Top-K metrics, which undercuts the 'robust and general framework' claim.

The closest related work—Yuan et al. (2026), diffusion LLMs for BBO—is excluded from the main comparison on the grounds of a different data regime (npool=10 vs. 500), which is not persuasive: running their inference-only method at npool=500 would directly test whether parameter updating is needed at all.

Some results are suspicious or under-explained: the AR baseline on Ant reports 0.934 ± 0.000 (zero variance across 8 seeds), and the RL-only variant on TF Bind 8 achieves 0.437 ± 0.001 with no discussion of why variance collapses.

The 'small-data setting' framing is somewhat overstated: the method trains on 16,384 samples per stage derived from only 500 designs with oracle labels used to construct responses whose labels exceed all prompt examples; this heavy reuse of a tiny pool raises questions about whether the model is genuinely optimizing or memorizing/interpolating high-label regions, and no analysis of generated-design novelty or distributional coverage is provided.

Continuous tasks are handled by rendering 60/56-dimensional float vectors as text with three decimal places, a representation that likely caps performance (consistent with DiBO losing to ExPT on D'Kitty), yet the paper still claims strong performance in 'continuous domains.'

The code link is a placeholder ('available here'), limiting verifiability of the many pipeline details (masking schedule interplay with delimiter tokens, response construction, similarity kernel) on which results depend.

strengths: The core idea—adapting diffusion LLMs (bidirectional modeling) to offline BBO via domain adaptation, SFT, and RL with label-improvement rewards—is well-motivated and clearly presented, with the delimiter-token unified corpus being a sensible mechanism for handling heterogeneous prompts, designs, and labels.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: 8 random seeds, 15+ baselines spanning forward, inverse, autoregressive, and diffusion methods, median/Top-K metrics, three additional RNA tasks, and extensive hyperparameter-sensitivity analyses (context length, pool size, RL learning rate, prompt paraphrases).

The matched diffusion-vs-AR backbone comparison (Table 2) is the strongest ablation, holding prompt construction, data, delimiters, and the full pipeline fixed while swapping only the backbone—this directly tests the central hypothesis rather than relying on cross-paper comparisons.

The authors proactively address contamination concerns with a behavioral ranking-probing audit (Appendix A.7) showing the pretrained checkpoint does not already encode design-label knowledge, and they strengthen GP baselines with dimension-scaled priors (Appendix A.4) rather than using weak strawmen.

Good reproducibility posture: implementation details (learning rates, batch sizes, optimizer, sample counts per stage), full prompt instantiations, and data-construction procedures (D1/D2 partitioning, similarity-conditioned context) are documented, with code released.
weaknesses: The central bidirectional-dependency motivation is only partially supported by the evidence. The diffusion-vs-AR gains are large on discrete DNA tasks (0.05–0.08) but essentially negligible on continuous tasks (0.001–0.015 on D'Kitty RL), and the paper provides no direct analysis or measurement of bidirectional structure in the design problems. The headline claim risks being a post-hoc narrative rather than a validated mechanism.

The 'state-of-the-art on Design-Bench' claim is overstated relative to the results. DiBO loses to ExPT on D'Kitty (0.923 vs 0.950 at the 100th percentile) and, more problematically, on the median metric for D'Kitty DiBO (0.837) trails COMs (0.887). The paper does not surface this in the main text, where Table 1 reports only the 100th-percentile metric prominently.

The primary metric (best of 128 candidates with duplicates discarded and generation continued until 128 unique valid outputs) is favorable to a high-capacity generative model and can mask weak typical-case behavior; while median/Top-K results are in the appendix, the main narrative rests on the 100th-percentile score.

Generalization evidence is limited: four Design-Bench tasks with N=500 samples, plus three RNA tasks where results are admittedly mixed—DiBO loses to both COMs and ExPT on most Top-K and median metrics for RNA-B and on several for RNA-A/C. The conclusion of a 'robust, general-purpose paradigm' goes beyond what the mixed RNA results support.

Several methodological choices are under-justified: the uniform old-policy assumption enabling removal of ratio clipping and KL regularization in the RL objective, the one-step unmasking log-probability approximation, and the omission of reward centering are each defended only by citation and intuition; no ablation isolates their individual effects (e.g., with vs. without the RL reward construction of Eq. 5).

The method requires an 8B-parameter pretrained LLM fine-tuned per task on an H100, which raises a fair compute-comparison question against specialized methods that are orders of magnitude smaller; the paper reports pipeline runtime but does not discuss this asymmetry.

Similarity-conditioned context construction (selecting prompts near the target response) is itself a nontrivial heuristic that materially affects performance (Table 5 shows up to 0.235 gain), yet it is presented as a design detail rather than examined for whether it constrains exploration or acts as a form of oracle-informed data curation.
